new_statements.rule_in_words: Anywa is a tone language (high vs low per Lusted; two tonemes per Hieda 1994; four-way per Wikipedia summarising Reh 1996). Most words are monosyllabic (CVC). In polysyllabic native words stress falls on the stem (root) syllable, i.e. the syllable containing the root consonant(s), not on the vocalic prefixes/suffixes (a-, o-, -o, -ɛ etc.): a'wal 'gourd', a'bila 'hut', 'rɛmo 'blood', 'ɔtɔ 'house'. In loanwords (Amharic, Arabic) stress can be on any syllable, i.e. it follows the source language.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords: stress can be on any syllable ('gimmira 'tax' < Amharic gɨbɨr; dʒa'baŋŋa 'policeman' < Amharic zebeŋŋa; alaatθ'kɛ̈ɛ̈r 'soldier' < Arabic ʔal askari).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in a short phonology sketch (5 pp.); tone is treated separately as the important prosodic feature (high/low, grammatical > lexical). No instrumental evidence; Lusted was an SIL-affiliated field worker and the sketch pre-dates the full description (Reh 1996), which was not obtainable and may not recognise word stress at all.
new_statements.identity_note: Lusted 1976 describes Anywa of Ethiopia (Gambela area; she names the dialects Adongo, Ciro, Lul, Openo but does not tie the sketch to one of them) = anua1242. Hieda 1994 is based on Akobo-river (Sudan) speakers of the same language. No separate glottocode involved.
